newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Middle East impasse opens door for EU diplomacy.
newsitem.headline: Middle East impasse opens door for EU diplomacy.

text.p: The failure of the Washington summit to push forward the peace process has given the European Union the opportunity to reassert itself in the Middle East, diplomats suggested on Thursday.

Many EU governments -- particularly France -- were angered by their exclusion from the Washington summit, but the 15-nation bloc is now likely to press for greater involvement in settling differences between Israel and the Palestinian authorities.
"We have a lot at stake in the matter," said one diplomat on Thursday, "and it is wrong to say that European involvement will muddy the waters."
Another school of thought suggests that Europe, with nothing to offer in the peace process, would be better off staying on the sidelines.

"At the moment the EU has no levers of influence," said Shireen Hunter, research fellow at the Centre for European Policy Studies, a Brussels think tank. "The EU would be better off contributing only when they (Israel and the Palestinians) have sorted out the current problem."
Many European diplomats say privately that the EU's presence in negotiations could balance what some perceive to be Washington's bias towards Israel.
While Washington has bankrolled Israel for years, the EU has slowly built up its financial assistance to Palestinian authorities to the extent that it is now their biggest donor.
Earlier this week European diplomats were careful to dismiss suggestions that they were angered at being excluded from the summit, but their actions suggested otherwise.
They hastily arranged a meeting with Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat on the eve of the summit and are now finalising plans for a visit by the so-called troika to Middle East capitals.
"The EU has appeared to be frustrated by its lack of influence," Hunter said. "But really, what can they offer? What can the EU do?"
The troika -- which groups the past, current and future presidents of the EU -- is the highest-level EU body that can negotiate day-to-day foreign policy issues.

Although critics of the troika system say it is only as strong as its membership -- currently Italy, Ireland and the Netherlands -- they admit it at least gives the EU some profile in crisis management.

The Washington summit, called by U.S. President Bill Clinton after the opening of an archaeological tunnel near Temple Mount in Jerusalem sparked violent clashes between Israeli troops and Palestinian police, fizzled out on Wednesday without conclusion.
Talks now move to the Middle East, where Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Arafat will meet face to face under U.S. stewardship.
While some European diplomats believe the EU should attend the talks on the sidelines, Hunter says they would be best staying aloof.
"I don't think European countries -- either as a bloc or individually -- can contribute at this stage," she said.
"Ultimately the U.S. is the only foreign player in this picture and the chance of Washington allowing third parties to interpose is remote."

EU foreign ministers issued their strongest-ever criticism of Israel on Tuesday, hinting that its participation in a Mediterranean trade agreement could be jeopardised without commitment to an already-agreed peace timetable.
But Hunter suggested the threat might be hollow. "The problem with this kind of a sanction is that, if you react too strongly, what do you have left to bargain with?"
Given Netanyahu's slim electoral majority, she said, "the Israeli government does not have the luxury of being able to show flexibility."
